The growing reliance on Industrial Control Systems (ICS) has made it essential to evaluate their performance under various conditions, including those with and without cybersecurity measures in place. To achieve this goal, researchers have developed ICS testbeds that simulate real-world environments. This paper presents a novel ICS testbed, known as the ICS Open-Loop Testbed (ICTB), which utilizes a combination of physical and virtual components. The ICTB is built on the OpenFWS platform, a cloud-based ICS testbed that allows for seamless integration of physical and virtual systems. The development process of the ICTB is thoroughly documented, highlighting its key features and capabilities. Additionally, the paper provides a comprehensive evaluation of the ICTB, which includes an assessment of its ability to support the evaluation of control systems and cybersecurity measures. The ICTB is found to possess several benefits, including its ability to facilitate collaborative research, reduce costs, and simplify the evaluation process of control systems and cybersecurity measures.

This study examines the capabilities of multi-agent reinforcement learning techniques, which employ value decomposition using a linear or monotonic approach. Our analysis reveals that these methods' representation constraints lead to suboptimal outcomes, and we validate this conclusion with numerical simulations. To bridge the gap between theoretical findings and practical applications, we develop an algorithm that adapts to these methods' limitations while remaining computationally feasible within the realm of multi-agent reinforcement learning. Our experiments demonstrate the practical significance of these results, comparing the performance of this revised algorithm with existing approaches for solving distributed zero-sum games.

A stereotype is a widely held, simplified, and overgeneralized idea about a group of people, which can lead to negative outcomes for its members, including the perpetuation of stereotypes through language. This study presents a new dataset of 1,111 stereotypical sentences, along with 2,800 human-generated relevance judgments, to evaluate the effectiveness of machine learning models in detecting stereotypes. The authors also propose a novel deep learning approach, Stereotype Detection with Multi-structured Feature Fusion, to detect stereotypes in sentences. The experiment results show that the proposed method achieves a 0.928 F1 score, surpassing a widely-used BERT baseline model. The authors also discuss potential applications of this research to address the spread of stereotypes through language.

We address the challenge of optimizing Remote Electrical Tilt (RET) through a novel approach that involves minimizing the total power loss while adhering to quality of service constraints. To achieve this goal, we develop a solution that incorporates a two-stage method, commencing with an initial power optimization stage and followed by an optimization loop. Within the optimization loop, we utilize a gradient-based technique, coupled with a trust region, to iteratively refine the tilt values. Furthermore, we establish a convergence criterion to ensure the proposed method achieves the desired outcome. Through simulations, we demonstrate that our tilt optimization method outperforms a conventional tilt setting and, when applied to a large-scale cellular network, yields substantial gains in terms of energy efficiency relative to the initial tilt settings.

A combined measurement of the CKM angle gamma is presented, obtained from the latest LHCb results for charmless B decays. The values of gamma are determined from the ratios of B decays involving pions and kaons, which are combined to yield a single value of 56.9 degrees with an uncertainty of 2.0 degrees, representing a tenfold improvement over the previous estimate. Further results are provided for gamma-related B decay rates and cos(2gamma) values, as well as a separate measurement of the angle beta, which is 21.0 degrees with an uncertainty of 0.6 degrees, based on B_d to D K decays.

In the context of complex n-dimensional space, we examine complex convex bodies, with a particular focus on complex ellipsoids due to their geometric properties as minimizers of the multiple Gaussian norm. These are characterized by being homogeneous with respect to the Gaussian norm. We derive the set of second-order partial differential operators that leave the Gaussian hyperball invariant, which results in a list of 16 distinct operators. These operators are then classified into four distinct groups based on their commutator relationships. We demonstrate that the four groups correspond to four categories of convex bodies, with complex ellipsoids being the unique category of convex bodies that are both cyclically and tangentially symmetric.

The collection of personal data by large tech companies has become a widespread concern, yet the views of the general public on this issue are not thoroughly understood. Our research aimed to clarify the complex dynamics surrounding data collection through surveys and interviews conducted with 11 individuals from various backgrounds and age groups. The participants shared their perspectives on data collection, privacy, and the benefits of data-driven technology. Our analysis of the findings reveals that people are ambivalent about data collection, acknowledging both its benefits and drawbacks. They propose a compromise between individual privacy and the benefits of data-driven technology, suggesting the creation of a system where individuals have control over their personal data. Our research findings provide valuable insights for tech companies, policymakers, and the broader technology industry.

This paper explores the potential of Faster-than-Nyquist (FTN) transmission in 5G New Radio (NR) downlink systems, specifically investigating how FTN signaling can be integrated with massive MIMO (mMIMO) technology to mitigate channel estimation and pilot overhead issues. To achieve this, researchers have developed a novel FTN signaling scheme that enables the simultaneous transmission of multiple antennas and subcarrier rates. To optimize the system's performance, a maximum achievable rate is derived and cast as a semidefinite programming (SDP) problem. However, to address the high computational complexity of the SDP problem, researchers have developed a low-complexity algorithm based on the iterative block coordinate descent (BCD) method. Simulation results demonstrate that the proposed FTN-MIMO system can significantly enhance spectral efficiency compared to traditional Nyquist signaling, specifically achieving a 30% gain in the strong channel environment.

A complete atomic lattice effect algebra (CALL) is defined as a type of continuous effect algebra (CEA) that exhibits complete and algebraic properties. Researchers have identified specific conditions necessary for the equality of two central elements within a CALL. These conditions are now applied to extend existing knowledge on the central element of a CALL. A new approach is also introduced to calculate the central element of a CALL using a specific operation. Notably, this approach is applied to a type of CALL associated with a unimodular groupoid, building on a concept first introduced by E.J. Moore. A specific subgroup of the automorphism group of this unimodular groupoid is also identified and its properties are explored.

This research introduces SaliencyMix, a novel data augmentation technique that enhances the performance of segmentation models by integrating salient information from images. The approach involves creating a mixed map by combining a random selection of unscaled region proposals from query images, which are then resized to match the query pixels. Unlike existing methods, SaliencyMix can utilize data from both high-quality and low-quality images, as well as salient regions that may not contain semantic information. Our experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of SaliencyMix in improving segmentation performance on various datasets, with the code available on GitHub.

The infinite-dimensional Iwahori--Hecke algebras $\mathcal{H}_\infty$ arise as a convolution algebra of bi-invariant functions on specific matrix groups. These groups, denoted $G_{m,n}$, consist of $m \times n$ matrices with an infinite number of upper triangular entries. The algebra $\mathcal{H}_\infty$ shares an isomorphic relationship with a subalgebra derived from the Hecke algebra corresponding to the group $S_{m+n}$. This research aims to understand the structure of $\mathcal{H}_\infty$ and its relationship to the symmetric group. It specifically demonstrates that $\mathcal{H}_\infty$ is isomorphic to a subalgebra of the algebra of double-ended quasimorphisms, a concept developed by D. Thurston. The study further reveals the structure of $\mathcal{H}_\infty$ and its relationship to the symmetric group.

The correlation between intrinsic shapes of galaxies, known as galaxy-galaxy shear, is a significant factor in cosmological studies that use weak lensing data. To address this issue, we have developed a new method to correct for intrinsic shapes by combining data from the Sloan Digital Sky Survey and the Baryon Oscillation Spectroscopic Survey. Our approach involves using a machine learning algorithm to accurately model the shape of the probability distribution of the galaxy-galaxy shear, allowing us to obtain precise measurements of the shape of the survey. By applying this method to a specific dataset, we have found that the shape of the survey is correlated with the shape of the data. Our results indicate that the shape of the probability distribution of the galaxy-galaxy shear is consistent with an elliptical profile, and that the shape of the survey itself is consistent with an elliptical profile. Our method provides a more accurate correction for intrinsic shapes than a previous method, and we have found that the shape of the probability distribution of the galaxy-galaxy shear is consistent with an elliptical profile. Our results also indicate that the shape of the survey is correlated with the shape of the data.

We investigate a class of soft, deformable particle systems that can be modeled by a Hamiltonian with a potential energy proportional to the square of the gradient. Under certain conditions, we prove that these systems reach equilibrium at a specific time point when they reach a unique stationary point. After this time point, the system's stress tensor and energy remain constant, exhibiting nonlinear elastic behavior under large deformations. This model can be applied to simulate various soft, elastic materials like gels and biological tissues.

To advance the development of gold nanoparticles with specific properties like biomedical applications, machine learning force fields are required to efficiently compute their structural and dynamical characteristics. However, the scarcity of experimental data for gold nanoparticles hinders the application of such models. We propose a novel approach to derive these force fields from first-principles simulations, which are then validated through ab initio molecular dynamics studies. This method enables the creation of machine learning models for various gold nanoparticles, which are then used to investigate their structural and dynamic behavior. We demonstrate that our model can accurately reproduce key features of gold nanoparticles, including phase transitions and melting points. Furthermore, the developed force field allows for the examination of dynamic properties, such as atomic diffusion, which is crucial for understanding the behavior of gold nanoparticles.

This paper leverages key concepts from variational methods, incorporating and expanding upon existing bifurcation theologies, Schauder's and degree theoretical findings, along with some novel contributions. We will apply these concepts to an equation system driven by the intersection of two nonlinear elliptic operators, one of which is in the form of a (p,q)-Laplacian, the other a p-pseudomonotone operator. We will demonstrate the presence of a countable set comprising bifurcation points, along with its properties, which consists of non-isolated solutions that have a stable nature.

A unifying concept for the lepton doublets, quark, and color fermions exists in the framework of grand unification. These fermions are grouped into families that each experience a common origin emerging from a gauge theoretical cause. This unification is achieved by incorporating a new gauge symmetry, which is then broken down into the standard model's unique gauge symmetry through the introduction of a new gauge field that transforms as a triplet within the standard model's framework.
We derive alternative representations of (h; q)-Genocchi numbers and polynomials using the fermionic p-adic q-integral on Zp, in conjunction with weighted q-Bernstein polynomials.

Randomized experiments are widely regarded as the definitive means of determining cause-and-effect relationships between variables. However, they are often limited to short-term effects and struggle to provide insights into the sustained impact of treatments across extended periods. To address this limitation, researchers have developed methods to extrapolate long-term effects from observed data by assuming certain conditions are met. Our study proposes a new framework for extrapolating treatment effects over time, which does not rely on the traditional assumptions of stationarity and can be applied in situations where the treatment's impact intensifies over time. We demonstrate that this proposed method aligns with the principles of causal impact and can be applied in both stationary and non-stationary environments.

To correct for recall bias, a method is proposed that combines a main study with an auxiliary study where the recall bias is assumed to be independent of the exposure of interest. This approach involves using a logistic regression model to estimate the odds ratio, which can be implemented using a single-stage estimation. Additionally, a semi-parametric method is presented as a variation for situations where the auxiliary variable is categorical. Simulation studies demonstrate that the proposed methods perform well in small to moderate sample sizes.

We introduce Autoencoders Within Flows (AEF), a class of latent variable models
that combines the flexibility of non-linear autoencoders with the benefits of
probabilistic distributions provided by flows. AEF models are constructed using a
series of coupled autoencoders, where the first layer is a probabilistic encoder
that uses a flow-based distribution to define the latent space, and the second
layer is a deterministic decoder that uses a flow-based distribution to
generate the input data. This setup allows for the use of standard optimization
algorithms, such as backpropagation, to learn the model's parameters. AEF models
are trained using a variational lower bound similar to VAEs, but offer several
advantages over their traditional counterparts, including the ability to learn
non-linear, high-dimensional latent spaces without resorting to reparameterized
gradients. Furthermore, AEF models can be trained using a wide range of
autoencoder architectures, including those based on convolutional neural networks
and U-nets, without relying on reparameterization tricks. We demonstrate the
effectiveness of AEF models in several applications, including image generation,
image inpainting, and image super-resolution, and show that they can be trained
more efficiently than VAEs and with fewer mode collapse issues.

Urban data collection through mobile devices has led to the development of innovative applications and services, leveraging city residents' daily activities to gather data and enhance smart city infrastructure. This research focuses on city government initiatives, allowing citizens to access data collected from their smart city applications. The proposed system, SmartCityExplorer, is designed to discover and visualize correlations between attributes collected from various smart city sensors. It utilizes a method called correlated attribute pattern mining to uncover trends and relationships within the data. The result is an interactive, user-friendly interface that presents data findings in an easily accessible and engaging manner, allowing residents to explore and learn about their city's smart initiatives.

We introduce a novel hybridizable discontinuous Galerkin method for solving the reaction-diffusion equations and the generalized Stokes equations in multiple dimensions. By utilizing a semi-discontinuous approach that combines low-order polynomial interpolation in space and a higher-order semi-implicit Euler method in time, our approach yields an H1-orthogonal system of equations. We then utilize a projection-based formulation to further reduce the dimensionality of this system, replacing the high-order unknowns with lower-order polynomial degrees that match the spatial discretization. By choosing these polynomial degrees carefully, our approach can achieve optimal error rates in both the continuous and discrete spaces, with numerical experiments confirming our theoretical findings.

A new method has been developed for conducting sensitivity analysis when the outcome of interest is missing and causal assumptions are uncertain. The approach, known as causal additive mixed models, is versatile and can be applied in a range of regression settings. We propose a novel method for calculating the probability of missing outcome data under specific missing data mechanisms, as well as a way to assess the robustness of causal inferences when the underlying assumptions are uncertain. Our sensitivity parameters can be estimated using Bayesian estimation and found to have a specific distribution. We also provide guidelines for choosing the distribution of these parameters. The method can be implemented using a new R package called cammix.

In crossover trials with missing gene expression data, a multivariate mixed-effects model is proposed, and maximum likelihood estimation via the Expectation-Maximization method is suggested. The approach is validated through simulation studies and applied to real-life study data.

We demonstrate that a particular structure on a category, which includes a collection of maps satisfying certain triangle and pentagon conditions, can be viewed as a categorification of a specific type of algebraic structure known as an A(n)-algebra. This is achieved by creating a family of higher-dimensional algebraic structures, which include a chain of simplicial complexes, and a monad that acts on this structure in a way that is consistent with the A(n) algebra structure.

DRAM is a memory technology that relies on a complex system of components, including memory channels, DRAM chips, and controllers, to function efficiently. These components have a multitude of adjustable settings that can be modified to enhance DRDRAM performance, reliability, and energy efficiency. This paper introduces a new DRAM framework called FlexDRAM, which empowers DRAM designers to fine-tune the internal workings of DRAM chips with ease. FlexDRAM achieves this by incorporating a programmable register that allows designers to modify the internal workings of DRAM chips in a flexible and efficient manner. The results of this study show that FlexDRAM can significantly improve DRAM performance, reliability, and energy efficiency.

The next-generation network architecture is likely to be driven by the convergence of computing and communication technologies, which will fundamentally alter the network's operation. In this context, networks will be able to perform various functions without relying on specific, physical components. This paper explores the implications of this shift on network management and control systems, as well as the need for updated modeling frameworks that can account for the dynamic and distributed nature of cloud-native networks.

In the context of quantum computing, fault tolerance is a critical issue, particularly in the context of quantum error correction.  A key aspect of this process is the ability to perform operations on multiple qubits simultaneously.  However, existing implementations of this method, such as the combination of logical NOT gates and a set of auxiliary logical gates, are not optimal.  A more effective approach involves using a combination of a set of auxiliary logical gates and a set of specific NOT gates, resulting in a more efficient method for fault tolerant computation.  This approach can be applied to both data and control qubits, and is particularly useful in the context of quantum error correction.
The OPUS system streamlines access to analysis and simulation tools by providing a unified interface, allowing users to easily run codes and offer customized computational services.

Engineering education has traditionally been limited by the lack of diversity in course materials, which often fail to cater to the unique learning needs of students. In an effort to break new ground, digital game-based learning has emerged as a novel approach to enhance engineering education. By leveraging immersive digital experiences, DGBL empowers students to engage in hands-on learning, which has been shown to improve their problem-solving skills, creativity, and overall engagement in learning. In this study, we conducted a comprehensive review of existing research on the application of DGBL in undergraduate engineering education, which revealed its potential to transform the educational experience. Our findings indicate that DGBL can lead to significant improvements in learning outcomes, although the quality of the learning experience remains a major concern. To fully harness the potential of DGBL, further research is needed to refine the design of digital games and other supporting tools, as well as to develop a more in-depth understanding of how DGBL affects the educational process.

The formation of molecular oxygen and ozone in the Earth's atmosphere is dependent on the rate of energy absorption from the sun's ultraviolet radiation. A novel method of modeling this process, based on the principles of random matrix theory, has been developed. This approach involves analyzing how energy is absorbed by the atmosphere and how it leads to the creation of molecular oxygen and ozone. A key aspect of the model is a random energy source that simulates the unpredictable nature of the sun's ultraviolet radiation. Our research shows that this model accurately reproduces the observed formation of molecular oxygen and ozone, and provides a new framework for understanding the complex interactions between the atmosphere and radiation.

We investigate the effect of impurities on stable counterflows in a three-dimensional lattice system with crosscurrents that are two-dimensional and resistant to distortions in space. These robust counterflows are characterized by their invariance to continuous deformations in space and can be represented by a set of Wannier bands with a specific band structure arrangement. We have found that these robust counterflows can withstand a significant number of random impurities in the lattice without losing their stability. Our study demonstrates that this stability is due to a combination of two factors: the inherent robustness of the counterflows to distortions in space and their resistance to distortions in time. We have also discovered that these robust counterflows can be preserved even when the lattice structure is time-reversed.

Recent advancements in multilingual neural machine translation have shown that a single model can translate multiple languages with varying levels of available data. This has led to the development of large-scale, multi-language models that can effectively translate low-resource languages. This study investigates the impact of training data quantity and linguistic similarity on low-resource Portuguese-to-English translation using a multilingual model. The results indicate that the model's performance is influenced by the presence of target-specific training data and linguistic proximity between languages. The findings suggest that the model can replicate the performance of individual language pairs with sufficient training data, and that it can outperform it in some cases when trained on Portuguese English translation alone.

The formation of dust particle acoustic waves in a dusty plasma system is studied using a two-temperature Maxwellian model for ions, coupled with the fluid dynamics of negatively charged and positively charged dust particles. At low charge-to-mass ratios for negatively charged dust, a specific type of ion acoustic wave is found to pass through the plasma system, whereas an unusual type of mode is discovered when this ratio exceeds a certain threshold. This mode is characterized by the interaction between the positively charged dust particles and the ions in the plasma system, resulting in a unique type of wave that propagates through the plasma.

Recent advancements in dense retrieval have led to the development of several methods, including the use of pre-trained language models in the finetuning stage. This approach has shown to surpass the traditional bag-of-words technique. This study aims to further enhance the performance of dense retrieval by investigating the effects of pre-training language models directly on the dense retrieval layer. We propose a new architecture that integrates the transformer encoder for both pre-training and finetuning stages. We also introduce a new pre-training objective that encourages the encoder to capture long-range dependencies within a query and its associated documents. This approach allows for the encoding of documents in a manner that is tailored to the query, thereby facilitating more effective retrieval. We have tested our approach on various datasets and found that it outperforms the current state-of-the-art dense retrieval techniques.

Multimodal learning's central aim is to create a unified understanding of diverse data types. This study proposes a novel multimodal learning framework, which leverages the connections between different data types to extract their underlying commonalities. By using a multimodal representation that combines a unified space with separate modes, the framework facilitates the model's ability to capture shared information. To achieve this, a unified space is learned through a two-way process involving a fusion operator and a disintegration operator. The fusion operator combines multiple modes into a unified representation, while the disintegration operator projects a unified space back onto its individual components. To ensure the model's ability to capture shared information, the fusion and disintegration operators are designed to be mutually compatible. The framework is further enhanced by incorporating a disentanglement mechanism that decouples mode-specific information from the unified representation. This results in a model that can focus on capturing shared information. The framework's effectiveness is demonstrated through experiments on multiple datasets, resulting in the state-of-the-art performance in multimodal learning tasks.

We investigate the properties of four-velocity-dependent vector and axial vector
currents in relativistic quantum mechanics. We use a Hamiltonian formalism to
derive the single-particle equations of motion, which are found to exhibit symmetry
properties under chiral transformation. In the non-relativistic limit, these
currents reduce to their well-known relativistic counterparts. We then calculate
expectation values for these currents in a state of pure momentum, and show
that their time evolution leads to a breaking of chiral symmetry. We also
examine the properties of the single-particle effective action and use numerical
methods to solve the resulting equations of motion.

This paper presents a spoken command recognition system that utilizes a tensor-train network model to efficiently encode acoustic features. The incorporation of a tensor-train network allows for a compact encoding of acoustic features, which is particularly beneficial in spoken command recognition. The proposed model is evaluated in spoken command recognition tasks, with the tensor-train network compared to traditional DNN and CNN models. The results indicate that the tensor-train network achieves a low memory footprint while matching the performance of DNN and CNN models in spoken command recognition.

This study provides a comprehensive review of quantum jump methods applied to open quantum systems, including those with non-Markovian behavior, with a focus on Liouville-von Neumann equations and Poincaré maps. By examining various types of dynamics, the review investigates the underlying principles of quantum jump methods and presents examples of generalised quantum jump schemes. Additionally, it discusses numerical methods for solving generalised quantum jump equations and highlights their relevance in fields such as natural science, engineering, and quantum information science.

The shape of nanoparticles in solar cell systems plays a crucial role in controlling the scattering and absorption of light. However, the interaction between these particles and the surrounding medium is complex, and traditional models are limited in their ability to predict the behavior of these systems. To address this limitation, a new approach is proposed that takes into account the optical properties of nanoparticles in different media. By combining the Mie theory and the FDTD numerical method, this approach is able to calculate the absorption spectrum of a system containing multiple nanoparticles. The resulting model is then used to optimize the design of a solar cell system that incorporates gold and silver nanoparticles, and the simulation results show a significant increase in solar energy conversion efficiency.

We investigate the complexity of fixed points within first-order logic, specifically in polynomial time, by addressing two key issues: the existence of fixed points and their computational efficiency. We introduce a new approach to proving their existence, grounded in model theory, which enables us to establish fixed point theorems that are more precise and encompass more classes of structures than previous ones. We also develop a comprehensive proof that demonstrates the existence of fixed points in polynomial time, with the added benefit of providing a constructive proof. Furthermore, our method is applied to several classes of structures, including those defined by bounded depth circuits, which leads to a novel separation between deterministic polynomial time and a refined version of fixed point logic.

Deep learning models, particularly LSTMs, have been extensively utilized in numerous applications, including NLP tasks. However, their high model complexity results in substantial computational requirements and memory needs. To mitigate this, we introduce two innovative LSTM architectures, namely the Memory-Mapping LSTM and the Memory-Compressing LSTM. By integrating a memory mapping layer and a memory compression layer, these models aim to decrease the parameter count and computational complexity. Experimental evaluations conducted on various datasets demonstrate that our proposed models achieve comparable accuracy to traditional LSTMs while significantly reducing their complexity.

This paper delves into the MAVLink communication protocol, highlighting its
vulnerabilities and offering a custom implementation that mitigates these issues.
The discussion begins by explaining the MAVLink protocol's structure and key
functions, then explores existing security threats and presents countermeasures.
Subsequently, we demonstrate the integration of TLS encryption with a
MAVLink server, showcasing its enhanced security capabilities through a
comparative analysis of both TLS-protected and unencrypted communication.
Lastly, we outline future research avenues that could further secure MAVLink and
MAVLink.

Understanding network behavior is crucial for designing efficient, large-scale distributed systems, which are susceptible to network failures and performance issues. This paper introduces a practical framework for evaluating network performance that considers various attributes of networks. It also examines the trade-offs involved in optimizing multiple network characteristics simultaneously. Furthermore, a comprehensive approach is presented to evaluate the performance of large-scale, distributed object storage systems, which reveals the impact of network properties on system resilience and performance. This evaluation also highlights the importance of considering multiple network attributes to ensure accurate assessment.

The Maxwell equations in four-dimensional flat space can be rewritten using the metric tensor $g_{\alpha \beta} = -1 + v_{\alpha}\varphi_\beta + \varphi_\alpha\varphi_\beta$, where $v_{\alpha}$ and $\varphi_\alpha$ are scalar potentials.  A specific class of self-dual Maxwell solutions can be obtained by setting $v_\alpha=0$, resulting in a set of nonlinear differential equations for $\varphi(x)$.  This paper investigates the existence of global solutions to these equations and shows that they can be obtained by setting $\varphi(x) = \varphi_0(x) + \eta(x)$, with $\eta(x)$ being a small solution to a specific nonlinear equation.  We have found that the solutions to this equation are stable and can be matched to solutions of Einstein's equations.  This allows us to show that the self-dual Maxwell solutions can be matched to solutions of Einstein's equations, resulting in a set of self-dual solutions to the Einstein-Maxwell equations.  These solutions are stable and can be classified as part of a broader class of solutions to these equations.

We're introducing a groundbreaking method utilizing cosmic rays and muons to scan and explore hidden underground tunnels and structures. This technique leverages the precise measurement of muon momentum and can determine the location of empty tunnels using a differential measurement approach. This paper will outline the concept, data analysis, and results of a study using a test bed, CERN's Buried Tower, in addition to discussing the potential for detecting voids in civil engineering structures like underground tunnels.

This research explores the relationship between parsing expression grammars and context-free grammars that incorporate ordered choice. We develop two translation methods from the latter to the former and demonstrate the completeness and effectiveness of these translations. Additionally, we examine how to directly represent some context-free grammars using specific parsing expression grammars with an unlimited number of distinct identifiers for alternatives.

In the context of a classical field theory, we examine the thermal radiation emitted by a moving charge in a medium with spatial inhomogeneities, using a semi-classical approach. By employing the Schwinger-Keldysh method within a semi-conductor model, we calculate the thermal radiation's power emitted in a specific direction, which is characterized by a specific angular distribution. The results of our calculations show that the thermal radiation's power exhibits a transition from an exponential temperature dependence to a linear temperature independence at very high temperatures. Additionally, we calculate the thermal radiation's power matrix and use it to determine the average direction of the emitted radiation, which is found to be proportional to the average direction of the moving charges.

This study examines how neural language models' predictions of word likelihood influence EEG recordings during a language prediction task. We compare three models of varying complexity to a baseline model, and discover that the more advanced models produce better fit results. However, these models do not significantly outperform the baseline in predicting EEG activity. We also find that the more accurate the models are in predicting upcoming words, the more informative their predictions are for EEG signal prediction. This study provides insights into the relationship between language processing and brain activity, and suggests that the models' predictions of word likelihood could be used to explain brain activity during language tasks.

Recent advancements in single-view 3D object pose estimation have been hindered by the reliance on artificially created datasets. This has led to overfitting and limited generalization capabilities. To address this issue, we present a novel method that leverages in-the-wild video data to develop a more robust model. Our approach involves utilizing video data to generate a more diverse and comprehensive training set, which is then used to improve pose estimation. To achieve this, we employ a two-step method that first identifies objects in video frames and then uses these labels to create a more robust training set. Our results demonstrate that this method outperforms existing solutions and can effectively mitigate overfitting.

In semiconductor-superconductor structures, nonlocal Andreev reflection plays a significant role in producing coupling between nonlocal Andreev states and localized normal states. This coupling is characterized by two distinct mechanisms: the exchange of energy quasiparticles and the transfer of Cooper pairs. We have investigated how these mechanisms influence the transport properties of hybrid semiconductor-superconductor nanowires by studying nonlocal Andreev reflection. We have found that the two mechanisms can be distinguished based on their energy dependence, and we have demonstrated how they contribute to the formation of bound states in normal-nanowire-superconductor-normal configurations.

Magnetic reconnection is a widespread phenomenon in space and astrophysics, 
involving the conversion of magnetic energy into particles and playing a key role in 
astrophysical plasmas where high-energy particles are produced. The mechanism behind 
this process is complex, with the rate of particle acceleration varying significantly 
in different scenarios. The current understanding of magnetic reconnection is 
insufficient to explain the high-energy particles observed in certain environments, 
such as the Earth's magnetosphere and the Sun. This article provides an overview of 
the current state of research on magnetic reconnection and particle acceleration, 
including the various mechanisms that have been proposed to explain the high-energy 
particles observed in these environments.

Extended scalar sector models, such as the real singlet extension, are being considered to explain the small mass of dark matter particles. We have calculated the one-loop corrections to the Higgsstrahlung process within these models, specifically focusing on the $pp\to h\to \gamma Z$ process. Our results show that these corrections can significantly impact the cross-section measurements, leading to increased uncertainties. To mitigate these effects, we have developed a simplified method to incorporate the one-loop corrections into cross-section calculations. Additionally, we have investigated the impact of these corrections on the Higgs coupling measurements and the constraints imposed by the Large Hadron Collider (LHC).

A key geometric property of the joint numerical radius is examined, yielding an explicit representation for the subdifferential of this quantity. This representation enables the computation of almost best approximations in a particular context.

As deep learning has become a crucial component in modern machine learning, its applications in finance have also increased, specifically in areas such as financial trading data analysis. However, the widespread use of such data without proper protection poses a significant risk to financial security. This study aims to explore the risks associated with financial data analysis and propose a novel approach to safeguard it. By examining the dynamics of financial data and understanding the relationships between different assets, we can develop a model that ensures the confidentiality of data exchange. Additionally, we demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed method in maintaining data security while allowing for accurate prediction and learning.

This research paper explores the structural properties of multivariate stochastic mappings that are defined by a second-order relationship. The study employs methods from Hilbert space operators and positive definite functions to establish a framework for analyzing these mappings. The main findings of the paper involve the identification of new types of Hilbert spaces and their applications in representing stochastic mappings, as well as the introduction of a multivariate correlation measure and its correlation kernel. The correlation kernel is shown to be a special type of stochastic mapping that satisfies specific conditions. The paper concludes with the derivation of several key theorems that describe the properties of these stochastic mappings, including their behavior under transformations and their connection to systems of linear equations.

Researchers have successfully ignited a high-pressure hydrogen-oxygen mixture, with a 4% hydrogen and 96% oxygen composition, using a laser pulse. The mixture, at an initial pressure of 0.8 atm, was contained within a cylindrical cell and ignited from a 1-mW laser beam. Studies have shown that a pressure increase of two or more times the initial pressure accompanies the flame, with a maximum speed of 1.5 km/s achieved. Experiments indicate that a seed electron plays a crucial role in igniting the mixture, with a 1.5-J laser pulse sufficient to ignite the mixture at a pressure of 0.8 atm but a larger pulse, at 5 J, is needed to achieve the same result at a pressure of 16 atm.

This research introduces a Boundary-Aware Segmentation Network (BASNet) that addresses the challenge of accurate object segmentation within complex image data. The proposed network architecture leverages a multi-path fusion module, incorporating a boundary feature network and a context path network to enhance segmentation performance. The boundary feature network is equipped with a novel boundary-aware loss function, which optimizes its ability to predict object boundaries, while the context path network is designed to capture deep-level deep high-frequency information, further refining the segmentation outcome. The network's performance is evaluated across various datasets, including MSB-7K, PASCAL-VOC2012, and Ade20, in comparison to state-of-the-art segmentation methods, with promising results demonstrating the efficacy of the BASNet approach.

The integration of Vehicle-to-Everything (V2X) communication into Connected and Autonomous Vehicles (CAVs) is seen as a key factor in enhancing situational awareness for safe navigation. However, the current state of V2X communication, based on the IEEE 802.11p standard, is considered vulnerable due to the lack of robust security measures. To address this concern, researchers have proposed alternative solutions, such as software-defined networking (SDN), which offer improved security capabilities. This paper presents a comprehensive study on the security features of SDN-based V2X systems, including an in-depth analysis of the most critical security threats and defense mechanisms. The paper also explores the potential benefits of SDN in mitigating these threats and highlights areas for further research in this field.

In this study, we examine the movement and distribution of non-interacting, weakly active particles near a boundary in a two-dimensional space with a confined area. The particles' velocities are influenced by a random, time-dependent force and a directed diffusion force. By analyzing the system's steady state, we find that an increase in the particles' activity leads to a significant increase in their density near the boundary. This increased density, in turn, causes a counter flow of energy, which is driven by the particles' activity. Our findings provide insights into how the particles' activity influences their movement in confined areas.

A novel approach to understanding electronic states in non-equilibrium plasmas utilizes Siegert states, a unified framework encompassing traditional energy states and quasi-particle states.  This concept is explored in-depth, with specific examples demonstrating its application to atomic processes such as photoionization, Auger transitions, and multiple-photon ionization.  Theoretical models for Siegert amplitudes are also introduced, allowing for the calculation of Siegert state probabilities.  Theoretical calculations of Siegert cross-sections and transition amplitudes are presented for these processes, with implications for plasma diagnostics and the potential for direct experimental verification also discussed.

Observations of the solar flare in the Ca II K-line reveal a pattern of fine structure in the emission lines, which shows correlated changes in intensity and velocity across various spectral components. This pattern is thought to be connected to localized plasma movements within the flare region, possibly resulting from magnetic reconnection. Our research suggests that the fine structure can be explained by the behavior of a plasma in a magnetic field undergoing periodic reconnection, which causes the emission lines to shift and change intensity due to the varying direction of the magnetic field. This model was tested using simulations of the magnetic reconnection process, which were then compared to the fine structure observed in the solar flare. Our results show a strong match between the simulated and observed patterns, indicating that the fine structure is evidence of the ongoing reconnection in the flare.

In this research, we investigate how the presence of a topological theta term affects the behavior of quantum chromodynamics (QCD) in the presence of a background magnetic field. Our investigation reveals that the presence of this term leads to confinement of color fields, preventing them from escaping even in the presence of a background magnetic field. This effect is distinct from the Aharonov-Bohm effect, which typically occurs in the absence of confinement.

The critical angle for ion beams was studied using a wide range of ions, including hydrogen, helium, and heavier ions with multiple momentum values. By analyzing the sputtered particle flux distribution, it was found that the critical angle is directly proportional to the ion's momentum and that the critical angle increases with the atomic mass of the ion. Furthermore, the data shows a linear relationship between the critical angle and the ion's energy, and it was observed that the critical angle decreases with increasing ion flux.

This research introduces an innovative method for source code anti-plagiarism detection that incorporates cryptographic techniques to safeguard against malicious tampering. The proposed system leverages hash functions and encryption to ensure integrity. The source code hash values are encrypted and distributed to a client, who can then determine the authenticity of source code by decrypting the hash and comparing it with its own hash of the code. The verification process is only successful if the hash values match, signifying that the code has not been altered. The same approach can be applied to prevent the unauthorized reproduction of audio watermarking systems.

We examine the connection between the degree of a Dirichlet series and the rate at which its coefficients increase, investigating the implications for the distribution of zeros of such series when counted with respect to a logarithmic scale along a horizontal line. Building on previous work, we refine and extend existing results regarding the distribution of zeros while broadening the applicability to Dirichlet series of higher degree.

We define a subgroup $E$ of a group $G$ as a $(k,r)$-metric approximate subgroup if it's a $(k,r)$-subgroup and satisfies the condition that for any element $e$ in $E$, the set containing the element raised to the power of $k$ and an open ball around $e$ with radius $r$, centered in $G$, is entirely comprised within $E$. We prove that if $E$ is a $(k,r)$-metric approximate subgroup, then the quotient group $G/\ker(E)$ is equipped with a $(k,2^r)$-metric approximate subgroup structure. We demonstrate that if the quotient group $G/\ker(E)$ is a locally compact group, then so is $E$. We also show that if the quotient group $E/\ker(E)$ is a finite group, then so is $G$.

We introduce a nonparametric method for estimating random variables with unknown log-concave densities in $\mathbb{R}^d$, leveraging a two-stage procedure combining a density kernel estimator with a conditional probability ratio. Theoretical analysis demonstrates that this approach converges uniformly at a polynomial rate, and experiments on simulated data confirm its practical efficiency.

We introduce a novel approach to studying granular dynamics on a scale that's large enough to be analyzed computationally. To do this, we use the Wang-Landau algorithm, which enables us to explore and sample static conditions in a granular system with a perfectly elastic sphere arrangement confined within a two-dimensional space. By employing this method, we're able to estimate the density of states for a system with a specific arrangement of spheres, and then use this information to calculate various physical properties, such as the system's energy and density. By gradually introducing spheres into the system, we're able to identify and track the formation of clusters and the development of a network-like structure within the granular arrangement. Our findings are consistent with theoretical predictions and provide valuable insights into the structure and dynamics of these granular systems.

In the game of "Explorer-Director", two players work together to find all N nodes in a graph. The "Explorer" aims to visit each node exactly once without using additional resources. At each turn, the "Explorer" chooses a new node to visit, and the "Director" decides whether the "Explorer" should visit that node next. At any given time, the "Director" has a list of the nodes that have been visited but have not yet been explored again. At some point, the game ends when all nodes have been visited. The "Director" aims to minimize the number of turns needed to achieve this goal. The complexity of this problem has been studied in various types of graphs. Specifically, it has been shown that this problem is NP-hard for general graphs, but it can be solved in polynomial time for trees and unit disk graphs. To tackle this problem, researchers have developed algorithms that use a resource allocation approach. The "Director" uses a resource allocation function to determine the number of resources allocated to each node, and the "Explorer" visits nodes with the highest resource allocation. These algorithms have been shown to be effective in solving the problem for various types of graphs. The "Explorer-Director" game has been shown to be a special case of the more general resource allocation problem, and the resource allocation algorithms can be used to solve this problem.
